## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
```
:::


---

## The question

Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a
sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a
statement about how wrong it might be.

Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won't.


## Instructions — delete this box




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
my_state <- "CA"        
my_variable <- "B25064_001"    
```
:::


## Pulling the data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
```
:::


Let's look at what came back.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dim(county_data)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```


:::

```

```

---

## How big is the margin of error?

A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000
than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a
percentage.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct =moe /estimate* 100)
```
:::




Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Sierra County, California        1181   705   59.7 
 2 Trinity County, California        922   220   23.9 
 3 Plumas County, California        1034   148   14.3 
 4 Mono County, California          1593   212   13.3 
 5 Mariposa County, California      1268   165   13.0 
 6 Calaveras County, California     1615   142    8.79
 7 Modoc County, California          818    71    8.68
 8 Lake County, California          1292   110    8.51
 9 Tuolumne County, California      1247   103    8.26
10 Inyo County, California          1140    88    7.72
```


:::
:::




Sierra County has the largest relative margin of error, with a moe_pct of 59.7%.

---

## Sorting counties into reliability categories


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    39
2 Low confidence      6
3 Moderate           13
```


:::
:::




Among California counties with valid rent data, 39 are high confidence, 13 are moderate confidence, and 6 are low confidence.

---

## Is the margin of error bigger in small places?

To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row.
That means a **wide** pull.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     2318     17 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California        NA     NA    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      1380    106   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       1369     31  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   1615    142   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      1139     67   21895    NA
```


:::
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))
```
:::


Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         39        989118.
2 Low confidence           3          6771.
3 Moderate                16         40430.
```


:::
:::





The average population of counties in the high-reliability group was 989,118, while the average population of counties in the low-reliability group was only 6,771. This pattern shows counties with smaller populations tend to have higher relative error and lower confidence in ACS rent estimates.

---

## What this means for policy



When using data from the ACS to analyze urban policy, we need to pay attention to the margin of error, particularly for small, sparsely populated counties. In California, counties with extremely small populations, such as Sierra County, have very high relative errors, so we cannot rely too heavily on rent estimates from these counties when making policy decisions.

The primary source of this uncertainty is the small sample size of the survey. Because the number of survey respondents is limited, the estimates are subject to greater variation.

Before applying census spatial data in urban planning work, we should check if these estimates are reliable. We cannot take every ACS figure as a hard truth. Recognizing estimation errors prevents us from making poor policy decisions that rely on shaky statistical results.
